🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +1.24% (intraday, 7-year -18bp). At trading day 34 (last close) it was +0.70% against a five-campaign average of -1.09% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.98%. The 10-year is -14bp since the hike vs a +16bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 784bp against a five-year average of 417bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +33bp and BB +15bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.37 → 0.68 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is untouched (+9bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,146bp, -8bp since 2026-11-03, 49bp under the Oct 15 record and 694bp over the June low. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 80.0 (15.0%, -4.8pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 145bp, Oracle 299bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -39%, NBIS -35%, IREN -40% vs NVDA -13%.

Wednesday's close (as of 2026-11-04 17:35 ET) was a broad relief rally. The S&P 500 rose 1.581467% to 7688.62, the Nasdaq Composite 1.436622% to 25736.51, the Russell 2000 1.582359% to 2856.95, and the Dow led with +3.030507% (+1569.4 to 53356.12). VIX fell 20.25924% to 16.61 from 20.83. Europe joined in: SX5E +1.971663%, STOXX 600 +1.818294%, FTSE +1.79331%. Japan did not: the Nikkei fell 1.415986% and the JGB 10Y rose 4bp to 2.821. The macro driver was energy. Brent fell 8.69691119691119% to 94.59 and WTI is shown -8.294307420126962%. Yields fell with it: US 10Y -7.42bp to 4.8879, 2Y -5bp to 4.5809, Gilt 10Y -13.2bp to 5.129, Bund -5.8bp. Leadership was cyclical and rate-sensitive: US Cons Discr +4.27%, Financials +3.46%, Real Estate +3.19%. Energy fell 4.77%. Info Tech managed only +0.55% and is still -5.9% on the week and -10.42% on the month. We could not verify the cause of the oil drop or the rally from same-day reporting (see the Iran section). The Newsquawk weekly calendar lists the US midterm election in this window. Sentiment improved from the prior session, and the computed rally watch now reads 'Spike-and-turn with calm credit is in place (rally conditions on)'. Its own history is a caution: trap_rate 0.5, typical trap gain 0.107 over 17.5 days vs real rallies at 0.324 over 106.5 days. The tech phase model is still in Phase 1 ('initial drop, credit calm', day 21 since peak). One signpost has TRIGGERED: 57.14% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs, against the 50% line. SOX is at -29.83% from its 52-week high, 0.17pp from the -30% signpost. The phase model's 6m odds are P1 0.54 / P2 0.251. It estimates a 0.563 chance of reaching Phase 2 or worse at some point within 12m. These are model estimates, not forecasts of certainty. Credit is the counterpoint. Headline US HY OAS is 3.35% (25th percentile) and IG is 0.91%. But the HY contagion read (as of 2026-11-03) shows the Caa-B gap at 784bp, the 99.69th percentile of its 5-year history, up 88bp in 1m and 219bp in 3m. Caa itself is at 1113bp, the widest since 2020-04-16. Some of that stress is reaching single-B: B OAS is up 33bp over 1m and 73bp over 3m to 329bp. Ba is up 15bp/1m and 48bp/3m to 200bp. IG is up 9bp/1m and sits mid-range on 5y history (47.5th percentile). The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen from 0.366 three months ago to 0.678, roughly back to its 5y median of 0.693. The read: CCC stress is leaking into single-B, but BB and IG are not yet repricing in a disorderly way. This is a descriptive gauge, not a validated signal. On AI credit, CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1145.98bp, 48.5bp below its 1,194.5bp Oct-15 record but 93.5% of the way up from the June low. It tightened 7.5bp on the day, and Nvidia CDS tightened 0.72bp to 144.93. The market is not yet testing Nvidia's backstop, but it is not pricing the neocloud risk away either.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 420.55 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 420.55 cents/gal, the 99.0th percentile of its history (z 2.64), and every one of the five signals sits at a high extreme and points SELL. The tightness shows up across the market: the crack spread is at 88.511 $/bbl (z 4.56), and the curve is in steep backwardation, with the front month 81.64 cents/gal over the 12th month and 157.81 over the 36th. That pattern usually means a physical squeeze on prompt barrels, and history says such squeezes tend to fade. The front-end spread and refining-margin signals carry the strongest edge, while the outright price signal points the same way but with a smaller expected move.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.52 vol points (20th percentile of the 60 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 93.9 (67th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 76bp (flatter by 9bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

Cup window fixed at 2000-present; swing detection uses a +/-6-week window on closes; cup pass = >= 90% retracement of the left-rim decline; ascending-triangle pass = slope>0, p<0.05, and >=60% of swing-low steps higher. This is pattern analysis of historical price data, not investment advice, and nothing here forecasts a level or a direction.

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 34 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Persistent but not re-accelerating at the core; the risk sits in the flexible/energy tail. Trend measures sit near the middle-upper part of their history and are mostly flat: Median CPI 2.61 (falling), 16% trimmed-mean CPI 2.66, Median PCE 2.67, Trimmed-mean PCE 2.26, Core Sticky CPI 2.78. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score is rendered separately. Headline Core PCE YoY at 3.12115 is above the trimmed/median gauges, so a few categories are pulling the average up. The Dallas distribution confirms a split basket. 26.8% of PCE items are running above 5% (16.6% above 10%), while 25.6% are falling. That is fat tails, not broad-based heat. Flexible CPI at 6.1232 (82nd percentile, rising) is the energy/volatile channel. Today's 8.7% Brent drop, if it holds, is the most direct relief for that channel. Expectations are anchored: 5y breakeven 2.2895, 1y 2.1026. Wages are not a driver: AHE 3.0%, ECI YoY 0.8. Net: core is sticky around 2.6-2.8%, above target and not falling fast. Persistence rests on a narrow, energy-linked tail that today's oil move works against.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analogy works best on conditions, not on valuations. The Nasdaq is nowhere near 175x earnings, and price stretch above the 200-day line is minimal (2.6%). This is not a blow-off top. What looks like 2000 is the backdrop: very tight IG and Baa spreads, loose financial conditions (NFCI -0.46), low VIX after today's 20% collapse, and capital crowded into equities versus commodities. Those are the conditions under which a tech drawdown can widen into a credit event. The phase framework says the bust has started at the leadership level. Info Tech is -10.42% and Comm Services -12.93% over 1m, and AI-infrastructure equities are deep in drawdown: CoreWeave -61.05% from its 52w high, IREN -67.99%, Nebius -47.11%, Oracle -49.59%. Credit has not followed. That is the Phase-1 signature, and the HY OAS (420/448bp) and Baa-10y (195bp) signposts are what would mark the move to Phase 2. Today's rally qualifies as a 'spike-and-turn with calm credit'. The computed history says half of these setups were traps (trap_rate 0.5). The model's historical tilt at this phase mix favours gold, Treasury duration and IG credit over mega-cap growth. The five inputs in this block (top-10 concentration ~40%, IPO froth 55, CAPE ~38x, market cap/GDP ~210%, LT EPS-growth expectations 65) are analyst estimates. We could not verify them from same-day sources and they should be refreshed. IPO froth is informed by 2026's mega-IPO pipeline (Goldman's projection of record US IPO proceeds; Cerebras' reported $5.6bn raise).

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the next meeting, with a hawkish-leaning statement. On record, Warsh's first meeting as chair left rates unchanged, the fourth straight hold after three 25bp cuts at the end of 2025 (MPA). At least one report said traders expected the committee to hike by December because oil was up about 30% YTD at the time (single source, unverified elsewhere). Our inference: with Brent down 8.70% today, 2Y yields 5bp lower at 4.5809, and core trend inflation flat rather than accelerating, a hike at the next meeting looks less likely than that pricing implied. We have no verified current market-pricing source.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his record (flagged as inference): Warsh has long argued for a smaller Fed balance sheet, less reliance on forward guidance and data-dependence 'theater', and 'regime change' at the Fed. He has also argued that productivity gains (including AI) can allow lower policy rates without reigniting inflation. Over ~1 year the likely mix is continued balance-sheet runoff or a reconfigured balance sheet, paired with a modestly lower policy rate if core trend measures drift toward 2.5%. That combination would steepen the curve. He chairs a 12-voter FOMC and faces public White House pressure for lower rates, so outcomes depend on committee consensus.

Warsh's Fed has so far chosen patience. Morningstar and CBS framed his tenure as a test between his long-held hawkish instincts on the balance sheet and political pressure for cuts, with Trump posting that 'The Fed should substantially lower interest rates, NOW!'. Today's data supports patience. Breakevens are anchored (5y 2.2895), core sticky CPI is flat at 2.7765, and payrolls are soft at 29. Flexible CPI at 6.1232 and Core PCE at 3.12115 argue against near-term cuts. The one-year view above is our inference from his speeches and writings, not a stated plan.

Sources: Fed issues the first rate decision of the Kevin Warsh era (MPA) · What Kevin Warsh as Fed Chair could mean for US interest rates (Morningstar) · 3 key questions for investors about Kevin Warsh (CBS News) · Fortune - Kevin Warsh, gravitas and political baggage
